title: Coconut Water vs Pedialyte: Which Rehydrates Better?
excerpt: Coconut water vs Pedialyte for hangovers, illness, kids, and exercise. Why sodium matters more than potassium, how they compare, and when to use each.
metaDescription: Coconut water vs Pedialyte: which rehydrates better for a hangover, a stomach bug, or kids? Sodium, potassium, sugar, and when to use each one.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Pedialyte is the better rehydration drink, and coconut water is the nicer-tasting, more "natural" one. The difference comes down to sodium. Pedialyte is built on the medical recipe for oral rehydration, with a measured amount of sodium and a small amount of sugar that help your gut absorb water quickly. Coconut water is mostly potassium, with a little sodium that varies a lot from brand to brand, and usually not enough to match what you lose when you're dehydrated. For a mild case of thirst, a light hangover, or a hot afternoon, coconut water is fine. For vomiting, diarrhea, a heavy night of drinking, or a sick child, Pedialyte (or a store-brand equivalent) is the one to reach for.

**The quick picks:**

- **Sick child, stomach bug, vomiting or diarrhea:** Pedialyte or another oral rehydration solution. Not coconut water.
- **Rough hangover with nausea or a lot of fluid lost:** Pedialyte.
- **Light hangover, or you just feel a bit dried out:** either works. Coconut water plus a salty snack is a reasonable choice.
- **You hate the taste of Pedialyte:** coconut water with a small pinch of salt, or a mix of the two, gets you closer.
- **Kidney disease, or you take medicine that raises potassium:** ask your doctor before drinking large amounts of either, and be especially careful with coconut water.

> **When to see a doctor instead of reaching for a drink.** Both drinks are meant for mild dehydration. **Get medical care if** you can't keep fluids down for several hours, you haven't urinated in 8 hours or more, you feel dizzy or faint when you stand, you're confused, you're vomiting blood or something that looks like coffee grounds, or you have a high fever with severe diarrhea. For babies and young children with vomiting or diarrhea, call your pediatrician for advice on how much rehydration solution to give, and get care quickly if a child has no wet diapers for 6 hours or more, is unusually sleepy, or has a dry mouth and no tears. **Call 911 right away** if someone who has been drinking can't be woken up, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, bluish skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, and no drink treats that. If you drink heavily most days and get shaking, sweating, a racing heart, or start seeing or hearing things within a day or two of stopping, that may be alcohol withdrawal, which can be dangerous. See a doctor or go to urgent care.

## Coconut Water vs Pedialyte at a Glance

Here is how the two compare on the things that matter for rehydration. Coconut water numbers vary a lot by brand, coconut age, and processing, so treat them as typical ranges. Pedialyte numbers are for the Classic ready-to-drink liquid. Always check the label of the exact product you buy, because both brands sell several versions.

| Per 8 oz (about 240 ml) | Plain coconut water (typical) | Pedialyte Classic (approximate) |
|---|---|---|
| Sodium | often 30 to 60 mg in packaged brands; up to about 250 mg in some | about 250 mg |
| Potassium | about 400 to 700 mg | about 190 mg |
| Sugar | about 6 to 12 g, natural | about 6 g |
| Calories | about 45 to 60 | about 25 |
| Designed for | a pleasant drink | medical oral rehydration |
| Taste | mild, sweet, nutty | salty-sweet, an acquired taste for many adults |
| Cost | moderate | moderate; store brands are cheaper |

The single most important row is the first one. Sodium is what your body needs most when you're dehydrated, and it's what makes a rehydration drink work. Pedialyte reliably delivers it. Coconut water usually doesn't, unless you pick a brand with a high sodium content or add salt yourself.

## Why Sodium Matters More Than Potassium

To understand why these two drinks behave differently, it helps to know how your gut absorbs water.

Water doesn't get pulled into your body on its own. It follows salt and sugar. The lining of the small intestine has transporters that move sodium and glucose across together. When sodium and glucose go in, water follows them by osmosis (the natural tendency of water to move toward where more dissolved particles are). This is the principle behind **oral rehydration solution**, or ORS, a simple mix of salt, sugar, and water that the World Health Organization promotes for treating dehydration from diarrhea. It's often described as one of the most important medical advances of the twentieth century, because it lets people rehydrate by mouth instead of needing an IV.

The recipe works best when the balance is right:

- **Enough sodium** to drive absorption and replace what's been lost.
- **A small amount of sugar.** Enough to power the sodium-glucose transport, but not so much that it pulls water back into the gut and makes diarrhea worse.
- **Not too concentrated overall.** Modern WHO ORS is deliberately "reduced osmolarity," meaning fairly dilute, because more concentrated drinks absorb less well.

Pedialyte follows this pattern. Its sodium, potassium, and sugar levels are set close to the medical guidelines for oral rehydration.

Coconut water has a different profile. It's naturally high in potassium and low in sodium. Potassium matters too, and it's one of the electrolytes you lose through vomiting and diarrhea. But sodium is the one your body loses in the largest amounts through sweat, urine, and an upset stomach, and it's the one that keeps fluid in your bloodstream. A drink that's rich in potassium and light on sodium will hydrate you, but more slowly and less completely than one built around sodium.

## What Coconut Water Actually Is

Coconut water is the clear liquid inside young green coconuts. It isn't coconut milk, which is made by blending the white flesh and is high in fat. Coconut water is mostly water, with some natural sugar and a mix of minerals, mainly potassium, plus smaller amounts of magnesium, calcium, and sodium.

A few things to know when shopping:

- **The numbers vary a lot.** The mineral content depends on the coconut variety, how mature it is, where it was grown, and how the brand processes it. Two brands can differ several-fold in sodium.
- **Read the label for added sugar.** Plain coconut water has only natural sugar. Some flavored versions and "coconut water drinks" add sugar or juice, which can push them closer to soda.
- **"From concentrate" and "not from concentrate" both exist.** Neither is a big deal for hydration, but taste differs.

Coconut water has a long history as a rehydration drink in tropical regions, and there are even old reports of it being used directly as an emergency IV fluid in remote places when nothing else was available. That's an interesting bit of history, but it's not a recommendation. Drinking it is a different matter from medical use, and today we have purpose-built solutions for serious dehydration.

For a deeper look at coconut water on its own, see our guide to [coconut water for a hangover](/never-hungover/coconut-water-for-hangover).

## What Pedialyte Actually Is

Pedialyte is a brand of oral rehydration solution made by Abbott. It was originally marketed for children with vomiting and diarrhea, and it's still one of the most common products pediatricians recommend for that. Over time, adults discovered it as a hangover drink, and the brand now sells versions aimed at adults too.

The main versions you'll see:

- **Pedialyte Classic.** The original liquid. Closest to the medical oral rehydration recipe.
- **Pedialyte AdvancedCare and AdvancedCare Plus.** Similar electrolytes, with added prebiotics in some versions and, in AdvancedCare Plus, more sodium.
- **Pedialyte powder packs and freezer pops.** Convenient forms of similar formulas.
- **Pedialyte Sport and other adult-focused lines.** Built for sweat loss, often with a different balance of electrolytes.
- **Sugar-free or low-sugar versions.** Useful if you're watching calories, though some sugar actually helps absorption.

Store brands from pharmacies and big retailers often make pediatric electrolyte solutions with very similar formulas for less money. If price matters, compare the sodium, potassium, and sugar on the label. If they line up with Pedialyte Classic, they'll work about the same.

## Which Is Better for a Hangover?

Neither drink is a hangover cure. Rehydration only addresses one part of a hangover. The headache, nausea, poor sleep, and general wiped-out feeling come from several things at once, including acetaldehyde (a toxic by-product of breaking down alcohol), inflammation, disrupted sleep, and low blood sugar. Dehydration is part of the picture, but research suggests it isn't the whole story, and people who drink plenty of water can still be badly hungover. We cover that in more detail in [does alcohol dehydrate you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you).

With that said, fixing the dehydration part does help many people feel noticeably better. Here's how the two compare for that job.

**Pedialyte wins for a heavy night.** Alcohol suppresses a hormone called vasopressin (also called antidiuretic hormone), which normally tells your kidneys to hold onto water. With less of it around, you urinate more than you drink, and you lose sodium along with the water. If you also vomited or had diarrhea, the losses go up. Pedialyte's sodium-heavy formula is designed to replace exactly that kind of loss.

**Coconut water is fine for a light night.** If you had a few drinks and wake up thirsty but otherwise okay, coconut water plus breakfast will cover you. Your food usually supplies the sodium coconut water lacks. Eggs, toast with butter, soup, or anything a little salty fills the gap.

**Coconut water can be gentler on some stomachs, and rougher on others.** Some people find Pedialyte's salty taste hard to get down when they're nauseous. Others find coconut water's sweetness or richness upsets their stomach. One small study on exercising men found coconut water and a sports drink hydrated about equally well, but some people reported more bloating and stomach upset with coconut water when they drank it in larger amounts. Another small study found fresh coconut water was well tolerated, with less nausea and fullness than a sports drink. The honest summary is that stomach tolerance is personal. Sip slowly whichever you choose.

**The practical answer:** pick the one you'll actually drink. A drink that stays in your stomach beats a "better" one you can't finish. If you're nauseous and can only manage small sips, Pedialyte freezer pops or ice chips made from either drink can be easier.

For a full playbook on fluids the morning after, see [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking).

## Which Is Better for Dehydration From Illness?

This one isn't close. For vomiting, diarrhea, or a stomach bug, **an oral rehydration solution like Pedialyte is the right choice, and coconut water is not a good substitute.**

Here's why. Diarrhea in particular drains sodium. A drink that's low in sodium doesn't replace it well, and the sugar in some coconut waters and juices can make diarrhea worse if the overall balance is off. Medical guidance for dehydration from diarrhea points to oral rehydration solutions specifically, not juices, sodas, sports drinks, or coconut water.

If you're sick and coconut water is all you have, it's better than nothing, especially paired with salty crackers or broth. But if you can get an ORS, use it.

## Which Is Better for Kids?

For a child who's vomiting or has diarrhea, use Pedialyte or another pediatric oral rehydration solution, and follow the label or your pediatrician's guidance on how much and how often. Small, frequent sips (a spoonful every few minutes for a young child) tend to work better than big gulps, which can trigger more vomiting.

Coconut water isn't designed for this, its sodium is too unpredictable, and its potassium content can be high for a small body. A healthy child having some coconut water as a drink is fine. A sick, dehydrated child should get a proper rehydration solution.

For babies, don't give either one without talking to your pediatrician first. Infants become dehydrated quickly and need medical guidance on fluids.

## Which Has More Electrolytes?

It depends which electrolyte you mean, and that's where a lot of the marketing confusion comes from.

- **Potassium:** coconut water usually has much more. One cup can carry two to three times the potassium of the same amount of Pedialyte Classic.
- **Sodium:** Pedialyte usually has more, often several times more than packaged coconut water.
- **Total electrolytes:** coconut water can look impressive on paper if you add up all the minerals, but that's mostly potassium. For rehydration, the sodium number is the one that counts most.

So when a coconut water brand says it has "more electrolytes than a sports drink," it may be true on potassium while being false on sodium. Look at the sodium line on the label.

## Which Is Better for Exercise and Heat?

For a normal workout of an hour or less, plain water is usually enough, and coconut water is a pleasant alternative if you like it. For long, sweaty sessions or hot days, sweat drains a lot of sodium, so a drink with real sodium content does a better job. Pedialyte, an electrolyte powder, or salty food alongside your drink all work. Coconut water alone tends to fall short on sodium for heavy sweaters.

If you want to make your own, our [homemade electrolyte drink](/never-hungover/homemade-electrolyte-drink) guide covers simple recipes, including ones that use coconut water as a base.

## How to Make Coconut Water Work Better

If you prefer coconut water, you don't have to give it up. A few small changes make it a much better rehydration drink:

1. **Add a small pinch of salt.** About an eighth of a teaspoon of table salt per 8 to 12 ounces adds a meaningful amount of sodium. Taste it. It should taste faintly salty, not like seawater.
2. **Pick a higher-sodium brand.** Check labels and compare. Some brands carry several times the sodium of others.
3. **Eat something salty with it.** Crackers, pretzels, broth, eggs, or toast with butter cover the sodium gap on their own.
4. **Mix it with Pedialyte.** Some people cut Pedialyte with coconut water to soften the taste. You lose some precision, but it's still a sodium-containing drink that's easier to finish.
5. **Stick to plain, unsweetened coconut water.** Skip versions with added sugar or juice.

## Who Should Be Careful With Coconut Water

Coconut water is safe for most healthy people in normal amounts. The concern is potassium. Your kidneys normally get rid of extra potassium easily, but if they can't, potassium can build up in the blood, which can cause dangerous heart rhythm problems. There are published case reports of people developing high potassium after drinking very large amounts of coconut water.

Be careful, and talk to your doctor before drinking large amounts, if you:

- Have **kidney disease** or reduced kidney function
- Take **medicines that raise potassium**, such as ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone, or other potassium-sparing diuretics
- Take **potassium supplements**
- Have **heart failure** or have been told to limit potassium

A glass now and then is very unlikely to be a problem for most people. It's the "drink a liter or two to rehydrate" approach that can add up.

## Who Should Be Careful With Pedialyte

Pedialyte is also safe for most people when used as directed. A few things to keep in mind:

- **If you're on a sodium-restricted diet** for high blood pressure, heart failure, or kidney disease, ask your doctor how much is okay.
- **If you have diabetes,** check the sugar content of the version you buy, and consider a lower-sugar option, though remember that a small amount of sugar is part of what makes it work.
- **Don't dilute it or mix it with juice or soda,** because that changes the balance the formula depends on. (Mixing with coconut water is a trade-off some people accept for taste. It won't be as precise.)
- **Don't make it more concentrated** by using less water with powder packs. A stronger drink isn't a better one.

## Cost and Convenience

Both drinks are easy to find in US grocery stores and pharmacies. Prices vary by store and size, so we won't quote exact numbers, but a few patterns hold:

- **Store-brand electrolyte solutions** are usually the cheapest way to get a Pedialyte-style formula.
- **Powder packs** are cheaper per serving and easier to carry than bottles, which makes them handy for travel or keeping in a bag.
- **Coconut water** is usually priced somewhere between a sports drink and Pedialyte, with premium brands costing more.

If you're stocking up specifically for hangovers or the occasional stomach bug, a box of powder packs or a couple of store-brand bottles in the cupboard covers most situations.

## How Pedialyte and Coconut Water Compare to Other Options

If you're comparing more broadly, here's how these two fit in:

- **Water:** fine for mild thirst, but it has no sodium, so it rehydrates less efficiently after big losses.
- **Sports drinks like Gatorade:** more sugar and less sodium than Pedialyte. Fine for exercise, less ideal for illness. See our [Pedialyte vs Gatorade comparison](/never-hungover/pedialyte-vs-gatorade-hangover).
- **Electrolyte powders like Liquid I.V.:** usually higher in sodium and sugar than Pedialyte Classic, designed for adults. See [Liquid I.V. vs Pedialyte](/never-hungover/liquid-iv-vs-pedialyte-for-hangover).
- **Electrolit:** a Mexican oral rehydration drink similar to Pedialyte, popular for taste. See [Electrolit vs Pedialyte](/never-hungover/electrolit-vs-pedialyte).

For a side-by-side of the main options, our [electrolyte drinks for hangover comparison](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared) covers them in one place.

## Beyond Rehydration: The Rest of a Hangover

Rehydration helps, but it only treats one piece of the problem. A few other things make a real difference:

- **Drink less, and slower.** It's the only approach with solid evidence. Alternating each drink with a glass of water helps you pace yourself and limits fluid losses before they start.
- **Eat before and while drinking.** Food slows how fast alcohol enters your bloodstream.
- **Sleep.** Alcohol fragments sleep, which is a big part of why you feel wrecked the next day. Give yourself time to rest.
- **Go easy on painkillers.** If you need one, read the label and avoid stacking products. Acetaminophen is hard on the liver after heavy drinking, and ibuprofen and aspirin can irritate the stomach.

Some people also add a DHM supplement. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the evidence comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven. There is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers on its own, and it doesn't replace eating, drinking water, or drinking less. If you want to try it alongside your rehydration routine, a widely used option is [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), and a budget pick is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. For the habits that matter most, see [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## The Bottom Line

- **Pedialyte is the better rehydration drink** because it's built around sodium in the balance your gut absorbs best.
- **Coconut water is a pleasant, milder option** that's rich in potassium but usually low in sodium. It's fine for light thirst or a mild hangover, especially with salty food or a pinch of salt.
- **For vomiting, diarrhea, or a sick child, use an oral rehydration solution,** not coconut water.
- **If you have kidney disease or take potassium-raising medicines,** be cautious with large amounts of coconut water and ask your doctor.
- **Neither one cures a hangover.** They help with the dehydration part, and that's all.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is coconut water as good as Pedialyte?**

Not for serious rehydration. Pedialyte is built on the medical oral rehydration recipe, with a measured amount of sodium and sugar that helps your gut absorb water quickly. Coconut water is high in potassium but usually low in sodium, so it rehydrates less efficiently after big fluid losses. For mild thirst or a light hangover, coconut water is fine, especially with salty food.

**Is coconut water or Pedialyte better for a hangover?**

Pedialyte is better after a heavy night, especially if you vomited or feel very dried out, because it replaces the sodium alcohol makes you lose. Coconut water is fine after a lighter night if you pair it with breakfast. Neither one cures a hangover. They only help with the dehydration part, not the headache, nausea, or poor sleep caused by alcohol's other effects.

**Can I give my child coconut water instead of Pedialyte?**

For a child who's vomiting or has diarrhea, use Pedialyte or another pediatric oral rehydration solution, and follow the label or your pediatrician's directions. Coconut water's sodium content is too low and unpredictable to replace what a sick child loses. For babies, talk to your pediatrician before giving either. Get care quickly if a child has no wet diapers for 6 hours or more or seems unusually sleepy.

**Which has more electrolytes, coconut water or Pedialyte?**

Coconut water usually has more potassium, often two to three times as much per cup. Pedialyte usually has much more sodium. For rehydration, sodium matters most, so Pedialyte is the stronger rehydration drink even if coconut water's total mineral count looks impressive on the label.

**Can I add salt to coconut water to make it like Pedialyte?**

You can get closer. About an eighth of a teaspoon of table salt per 8 to 12 ounces of plain coconut water adds a useful amount of sodium. It won't match a medical oral rehydration solution exactly, so for illness or a sick child, stick with Pedialyte or a pharmacy store brand. For a mild hangover or a hot day, salted coconut water works well.

**Is it safe to drink a lot of coconut water?**

For most healthy people, normal amounts are fine. Very large amounts can raise blood potassium, which is risky for people with kidney disease or who take medicines that raise potassium, such as ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or spironolactone. There are published case reports of dangerously high potassium after heavy coconut water intake. If any of that applies to you, ask your doctor how much is safe.

**Can I mix coconut water and Pedialyte?**

Some people do, to make Pedialyte's salty taste easier to drink. It's not dangerous, but it changes the balance of the formula, so it won't be as precise as Pedialyte alone. If you're rehydrating after an illness, drink Pedialyte as labeled. For a hangover, a mix you'll actually finish is better than a bottle you can't stomach.
